positions.source_passage:
I ask the FDA to make an important principle part of medical AI development: AI should search for and evaluate the full body of credible medical evidence globally and impartially—not rely predominantly on conventional U.S. pharmaceutical and medical literature.

This should include conventional medicine, complementary and traditional medicine, acupuncture, homeopathy, herbal medicine, nutritional therapies, and naturally derived substances studied in Europe, the Middle East, Asia, India, and elsewhere.

This does not mean AI should assume these treatments work. Quite the opposite. AI should evaluate them by the same rigorous standards applied to conventional treatments.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that evaluation standards for medical AI may rely on a narrow evidence base drawn from conventional U.S. databases, omitting credible international research and applying inconsistent or unequal treatment to different categories of evidence and therapies.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt medical AI standards that require broad evidence retrieval beyond conventional U.S. databases, inclusion of credible international research (Europe, Middle East, Asia, India, elsewhere), consistent grading tiers of evidence, and evaluation of conventional, complementary, and traditional treatments under the same standards.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges FDA to add elements to medical AI evaluation standards: evidence retrieval beyond conventional U.S. databases, inclusion of credible international research, consistent grading across study types from anecdotal to replicated trials, and equal comparative evaluation of conventional, complementary, and traditional treatments.
positions.source_passage:
I therefore encourage the FDA to consider medical AI standards that include:

Broad evidence retrieval beyond a limited set of conventional U.S. databases.
International evidence, including credible research from Europe, the Middle East, Asia, India, and elsewhere.
Consistent evidence grading, distinguishing anecdotal reports, laboratory and animal studies, observational studies, randomized trials, systematic reviews, and replicated clinical evidence.
Fair comparative evaluation of conventional, complementary, and traditional treatments using the same standards.
